findings.summary: THE TASK'S HEADLINE CRITERION HAS NO FALSIFYING TEST, and this is MEASURED rather than argued. M4.6d's row says the unleased epoch-0 commit path 'must GO, not merely be passed an epoch', because it is a silent FORK. Nothing in the suite pins that DefaultIngest's commits now land under a LEASED epoch. I restored the fork in production -- added back `private final CommitLog unleased = new CommitLog(store, prefix); unleased.recover();`, committed to it instead of the sequencer, and left the Sequencer field constructed, held and closed -- and the whole of `:ingest:test` was BUILD SUCCESSFUL, both new shutdown tests included. Every existing assertion survives it: the per-flush PUT count is identical (one delta object either way), `theFirstAppendAfterARestartCostsTheSameAsAnyOther` still passes because the epoch-0 log recovers itself and its own docstring says offsets continue with or without recovery, and `closeReleasesTheLease...` still passes because `sequencer.close()` still runs. No ingest test asserts anything about the commit-log KEY or the epoch in it -- `grep -n 'ctl/log|epoch' ingest/src/test/**` returns nothing. Three lines would kill it: after a flush, assert the delta object exists under the leased epoch's prefix (or, equivalently, that NO object exists under `<prefix>/ctl/log/<slot>/0000000000000000/` once the pod has flushed). ⚠️ M4.6f (deleting the 2-arg constructor) would make the mutant unrepresentable instead -- gate-design rung 1 -- but it is deferred, so as of THIS commit the criterion is unpinned by either route, and the M4.6f row's own words are 'a default nobody reaches today is a default the next wiring commit reaches by accident'.
findings.failure_scenario: A later wiring commit, a merge resolution, or a 'fast path' reintroduces `new CommitLog(store, prefix)` inside DefaultIngest. The suite stays green, the pod acks records into the reserved epoch-0 chain, and no reader at epoch >= 1 ever lists that prefix -- records acknowledged and never visible, plus offsets re-issued by the leader that the fork already assigned (I2 and I3). This is precisely the fork M4.6d exists to end, and the commit that ends it leaves nothing behind that would notice its return.

findings.summary: THE NEW `sequencer.close()` HAS NO FAILURE-PATH TEST (testing.md rule 14), and its placement makes that gap consequential. It sits in the `finally` of the try whose body is `flushNow()`. Before this commit that `finally` contained only `drainPushes()`, which declares no checked exception and cannot throw -- so a failed final flush ALWAYS propagated. Now a failed release REPLACES it: `flushNow()` throws IOException A, `sequencer.close()` throws IOException B, B propagates and A is lost with no `addSuppressed`. The javadoc twenty lines below (drainPushes, `DefaultIngest.java:438-443`) records this repository already paying for exactly this defect -- 'an unchecked throw from a finally escaped every catch (IOException) while masking a failed final flush' -- and the same shape is reintroduced one statement over. VERIFIED SURVIVING MUTATION: replacing the line with `try { sequencer.close(); } catch (IOException swallowed) { }` leaves all of `:ingest:test` BUILD SUCCESSFUL, so the tests cannot distinguish 'a release failure is reported' from 'a release failure is silently ignored' either. A store that rejects the release (stale CAS version after a self-fence -- LeaseManager's own javadoc says `release` can lose its version -- or a 503 at shutdown) exercises both halves, and a fake store refusing one PUT is a T1 test.
findings.failure_scenario: A pod shuts down; the final flush fails (store full, throttled, key rejected) AND the release also fails. The operator sees only 'could not release the lease at epoch N'; the lost final segment is silently discarded and the append that was waiting on it is completed by the pending-drain with a generic message. No test fails. Symmetrically, a future 'fix' that swallows the release failure passes every test while making a graceful shutdown that did NOT hand the lease back indistinguishable from one that did -- which is the whole property the sibling test claims to establish.

findings.summary: THE NEW SHARED FIXTURE'S ONLY STATED JUSTIFICATION IS FALSE AT ITS NAMED EXEMPLAR. `TestSequencers`' class javadoc, and the copy of it at `IngestTestSupport.java:75`, and the comment added at `http/build.gradle.kts:113-116`, all rest the 'a REAL LocalSequencer, not FakeSequencer' decision on `IntervalPutRateTest` counting a commit-log append among the PUTs in ADR-0016's table. `IntervalPutRateTest` constructs no DefaultIngest, no Sequencer and no CommitLog -- it drives `Accumulator` + `SegmentPublisher` directly -- and its own javadoc states the opposite in capitals: 'ONLY SegmentPublisher, no CommitLog ... a commit-log append is a SEPARATE request the cost table does not fold into that figure, and including it here would measure something the SPEC never claimed.' The rest of the sentence is no better checked: of the six call sites this fixture was created to de-duplicate, `MemoryFlatUnderTenXBodySizeTest` asserts heap only, `BulkThroughTheRealStackTest` wraps a CountingBinStore and never reads `counts()`, and the three plugin ITs count nothing. Only `MemoryFlatAtIntervalCeilingTest` is rate-sensitive at all, and it judges FILES walked on disk rather than requests, so the claim is right about that one for the wrong reason. The row this commit implements says the six pasted copies carried 'the same pasted rationale ... which was true of two of the six and false of the rest'; centralising the paste kept the falsehood and gave it one authoritative address. This is the class of defect the M4.6c row names verbatim: a comment claiming a mechanism it does not have.
findings.failure_scenario: The next author reads the fixture, believes a real leased sequencer is required wherever DefaultIngest appears, and wires one into a test that needs only offsets -- buying a wall-clock lease TTL, a lease object, a chain recovery and a per-flush commit-log object in a T1/T2 test, and the fixture's throw-on-held-lease when a test legitimately wants two ingesters over one store. Because the stated reason cannot be checked (its exemplar documents the opposite), nobody can tell which call sites actually need it, so nobody ever downgrades any of them to FakeSequencer. The correct statement is narrow and checkable: the request-DELTA assertions in `DefaultIngestTest`/`IngestShutdownTest` (4, 4, 5, isZero) and the file cadence in `MemoryFlatAtIntervalCeilingTest` would move under a sequencer that writes nothing; everything else in `http` and `plugin` would not.

findings.summary: NOTHING CONSTRAINS THE COMMIT REQUEST'S IDENTITY. This commit adds a `long flushSeq` field (`DefaultIngest.java:63`) whose javadoc states an invariant -- 'Half the idempotency key, with podId (M4.10) ... every increment happens inside the drain that lock already serialises' -- and passes `podShortId` into the request. VERIFIED SURVIVING MUTATION: `new CommitRequest("mutant", 0L, published.key(), published.recordCounts())` leaves the whole of `:ingest:test` BUILD SUCCESSFUL, and by construction nothing else can catch it -- `CommitDelta`/`RunCommit` carry neither field, `LocalSequencer.commit` forwards only `segmentKey` and `recordCounts`, and `FakeSequencer` documents that it ignores `(podId, flushSeq)` until M4.10. So the argument swap, the constant, and the dropped increment all survive. Ten lines with a recording `Sequencer` (the seam already exists) pinning podId == "pod1" and flushSeq 0 then 1 across two flushes would close it. Recorded as minor rather than major because the value is inert TODAY -- no reader consumes it, and a hyphenated podShortId still fails at construction via SegmentPublisher's own validation rather than at first flush.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.10 lands dedup on (podId, flushSeq) and writes its tests against the Sequencer seam, where the key arrives correct. DefaultIngest -- the only production producer of that key -- has been emitting a constant, or a value burned on every failed flush attempt, since M4.6d. Every commit from the pod is then either treated as a replay of the first (data silently dropped) or never deduped at all, and the tests that were supposed to prove idempotency all pass because none of them go through DefaultIngest.

findings.summary: THE ANTI-VACUITY HALF RESTS ON THE WALL CLOCK. `closeReleasesTheLeaseSoASuccessorSequencesWithoutWaitingOutTheTtl` is genuinely falsifiable -- I dropped `sequencer.close()` from production and BOTH tests in this file failed, at IngestShutdownTest.java:107 for this one -- so the core is sound. The cost is that its exclusivity proof is a 10-second `Clock.systemUTC()` TTL: `TestSequencers.leases` hardcodes the system clock, and `TestSequencers.TTL` is 10s. `TestSequencers`' own javadoc says 'A test asserting anything ABOUT expiry builds its own LeaseManager with its own clock' -- this test asserts exactly that ('the released term's 10s TTL nowhere near elapsed') and does not. The fix is one fixture parameter: an overload taking a Clock, called with `Clock.fixed(...)`, under which the pod1 lease can never lapse and the released (already-expired) lease is still takeable, so both assertions become deterministic. testing.md rule 1 and rule 15 both point the same way.
findings.failure_scenario: A GC pause, a WSL2 stall or a loaded CI box puts more than 10 s between line 95 and line 102 -- with only `ingest.close()` in between, so the window is narrow but real. pod2 then acquires because pod1's lease EXPIRED, not because it was released, and the test goes green having proved nothing: exactly the vacuity its own comment says it exists to exclude, arriving through the door the comment does not consider. The wider window (>10 s before line 95) fails safe, which is why this is minor rather than major.

findings.summary: THE 4 -> 5 THRESHOLD MOVE IS INVISIBLE TO EVERY GATE, so its justification must be in the commit body and not only in the test comment. `check-test-integrity` scores assertion STRENGTH per test method, and `isEqualTo(4)` and `isEqualTo(5)` both score 3 -- so a threshold moving in the weakening direction is not something it can see, in place or across a move. It will fire on the METHOD REMOVAL from DefaultIngestTest.java:463, demanding a `Test-removed:` line, and that tag will document the move while saying nothing about the loosened bound. AGENTS.md non-negotiable 2 covers thresholds and has 'No script yet'. On the substance I agree with the change and the compensating test is adequate: `isEqualTo(5)` still kills a spurious sixth request or a doubled release, and the sibling test independently establishes that the fifth request is a lease HAND-BACK rather than any incidental stat or re-read -- I confirmed the pair also pins the ORDERING, since moving `sequencer.close()` ahead of the final `flushNow()` makes `closeFlushesWhatIsStillBufferedRatherThanLosingIt` fail. So this is process, not a hole.
findings.failure_scenario: The reasoning lives in a 14-line comment inside a test file. `git log` -- which is what the next person reads when the count moves again to 6 -- shows only 'a test was removed'. The next bump then has a precedent of a quietly-raised cost bound with no traceable argument, and the one gate that could have objected has already declared itself satisfied by an unrelated tag.
